issue: Emphasis misplaced: source capitalizes only "OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR" ("whose appointments are OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR in the Constitution(2)"); candidate adds capitalized "ARE" which the source does not emphasize.
replacement: The first of these two clauses, it is plain, merely supplies a way of appointing officers "whose appointments are NOT OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR in the Constitution, and which SHALL BE ESTABLISHED BY LAW." It cannot, of course, reach the appointment of senators. Their appointments are OTHERWISE PROVIDED FOR in the Constitution,(2) they are ESTABLISHED BY THE CONSTITUTION, and they will not need to be established later by law. Hardly anyone will dispute this.

issue: Fixed-term rule: "Chief Magistrate" should be "chief executive" (STYLE-NOTE). Source "the Chief Magistrate of the United States"; candidate keeps "Chief Magistrate", while the same paper (p4) renders "chief magistracy" as "chief executive office".
replacement: The way the chief executive of the United States is to be chosen is almost the only important part of the system that has escaped harsh criticism, or has earned any word of approval from its opponents. The most plausible of them to appear in print has even condescended to admit that the election of the President is fairly well guarded.(1) I venture to go further, and I do not hesitate to say that if the method is not perfect, it is at least excellent. It combines, to an eminent degree, all the advantages that one could have wished to see combined.(E1)

issue: Leftover "--" inside the quoted verse ("contest--That"); STYLE-NOTE requires the unspaced em dash. Wording unchanged.
replacement: "For forms of government let fools contest—That which is best administered is best." Yet we may safely declare that the true test of a good government is its aptitude and tendency to produce a good administration.

issue: Fixed-term rule: source "the Chief Magistrate of the Union" kept as "Chief Magistrate" while the same paragraph renders "magistrate" as "chief executive".
replacement: This chief executive is to be elected for four years, and he may be re-elected as often as the people of the United States think him worthy of their confidence. In these respects he is wholly unlike a king of Great Britain, who is a hereditary monarch and holds the crown as a family property that passes to his heirs forever. But he is closely like a governor of New York, who is elected for three years and may be re-elected without limit or interruption. Consider how much less time it would take to build up a dangerous influence in a single State than to build up the same influence across the United States. We must conclude that a four-year term for the chief executive of the Union is a degree of permanence far less to be feared in that office than a three-year term for the corresponding office in a single State.

issue: Fixed-term rule: source "the Chief Magistrate of the Union" kept as "Chief Magistrate", in the same sentence where "chief magistrate of this State" was rendered "chief executive".
replacement: The President is to nominate and, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint ambassadors and other public ministers, judges of the Supreme Court, and in general all officers of the United States who are established by law and whose appointments the Constitution does not otherwise provide for. The king of Great Britain is emphatically and truly called the fountain of honor. He not only appoints to all offices but can create offices. He can confer titles of nobility at will, and he has the disposal of an immense number of church positions. The President's power in this respect is plainly far inferior to the British king's. Nor is it equal to that of the governor of New York, if we judge the meaning of the State's constitution by the practice that has grown up under it. The power of appointment among us is lodged in a council made up of the governor and four members of the Senate, chosen by the Assembly. The governor claims, and has often exercised, the right of nomination, and he is entitled to a casting vote in the appointment. If he really has the right of nominating, his authority here equals the President's and exceeds it in the matter of the casting vote. In the national government, if the Senate should be divided, no appointment could be made. In the government of New York, if the council should be divided, the governor can turn the scale and confirm his own nomination.(3) Compare the publicity that must necessarily attend the President's appointments, made with an entire branch of the national legislature, to the privacy of the governor of New York's, who sits closeted in a secret room with at most four people, and often with only two. At the same time, consider how much easier it must be to influence the small number that a council of appointment consists of than the considerable number that the national Senate would consist of. We cannot hesitate to conclude that the power of this State's chief executive in handing out offices must, in practice, be greatly superior to that of the chief executive of the Union.

issue: Wrong meaning: source "can make denizens of aliens, noblemen of commoners"; candidate "can make citizens of foreigners". A denizen was a foreigner granted residence and some rights, not a citizen. Also (NIT, same paragraph) source "elective and periodical servants of the people" rendered "elected and periodically changing servants"; "periodically changing" is not what the source says.
replacement: The President of the United States would be an officer elected by the people for four years; the king of Great Britain is a perpetual and hereditary prince. The one would be liable to personal punishment and disgrace; the person of the other is sacred and inviolable. The one would have a qualified negative on the acts of the legislative body; the other has an absolute negative. The one would have the right to command the military and naval forces of the nation; the other has this right and in addition holds that of declaring war and of raising and regulating fleets and armies by his own authority. The one would share with a branch of the legislature the power of making treaties; the other is the sole holder of that power. The one would share in the same way in appointing to offices; the other is the sole source of all appointments. The one can grant no privileges whatever; the other can turn aliens into denizens, foreigners granted residence and some rights of citizens, and can make noblemen of commoners, and can create corporations with all the rights that belong to corporate bodies. The one can set no rules about the nation's commerce or currency; the other is in several respects the arbiter of commerce, and in that capacity can establish markets and fairs, regulate weights and measures, lay embargoes for a limited time, coin money, and authorize or prohibit the circulation of foreign coin. The one has not a particle of spiritual jurisdiction; the other is the supreme head and governor of the national church! What answer shall we give to those who would persuade us that things so unlike resemble each other? The same answer that ought to be given to those who tell us that a government whose entire power would be in the hands of the elected servants of the people, chosen at regular intervals is an aristocracy, a monarchy and a despotism.

issue: Fixed-term rule: "the Chief Magistrate himself" kept; same paragraph renders "chief magistrate" (monarch) as "chief executive". Use "chief executive".
replacement: But in a republic, where every public official ought to be personally responsible for his conduct in office, the reason that in the British Constitution makes a council proper not only ceases to apply but turns against the institution. In the monarchy of Great Britain, the council serves as a substitute for the forbidden responsibility of the chief executive, and to some degree as a hostage to national justice for his good behavior. In the American republic, it would serve to destroy, or greatly reduce, the intended and necessary responsibility of the chief executive himself.

issue: Mistranslation: source "should have made himself obnoxious to its resentment" (exposed to its resentment); candidate "offensive to its resentment" is not sense (resentment is not offended).
replacement: It may perhaps be asked how a short term in office can affect the independence of the Executive from the legislature, unless the one holds the power of appointing or removing the other. One answer to this question can be drawn from the principle already noted, namely the slight interest a man tends to take in a short-lived advantage, and the little inducement it gives him to expose himself to any considerable inconvenience or danger on its account. Another answer, perhaps more obvious though no more conclusive, comes from considering the influence of the legislative body over the people. That influence might be used to prevent the re-election of a man who, by honestly resisting some sinister project of that body, had made himself the target of its resentment.

issue: Source "sensible of the propriety of the measures"; candidate "aware of the wisdom of the measures" shifts "propriety" (fitness) to "wisdom".
replacement: It cannot be asserted that a term of four years, or any other limited term, would completely serve the end proposed. But it would contribute toward it in a degree that would have a material influence on the spirit and character of the government. Between the beginning and the end of such a period there would always be a considerable interval in which the prospect of losing office would be far enough away not to affect improperly the conduct of a man with a fair share of fortitude. In that interval he might reasonably expect that there would be time enough, before the end arrived, to make the community aware of the propriety of the measures he was inclined to pursue. It is probable that as he approached the moment when the public were to express their judgment of his conduct by a new election, his confidence, and with it his firmness, would decline. Even so, both would draw support from the opportunities his earlier time in the office had given him to establish himself in the esteem and goodwill of his constituents. He could then take risks safely, in proportion to the proofs he had given of his wisdom and integrity, and to the claim he had earned to the respect and attachment of his fellow citizens. On the one hand, then, a term of four years will contribute enough to the firmness of the Executive to make it a very valuable ingredient in the composition. On the other hand, it is not enough to justify any alarm for public liberty. Consider the British House of Commons. From the most feeble beginnings, FROM THE MERE POWER OF ASSENTING OR DISAGREEING TO THE IMPOSITION OF A NEW TAX, it has by rapid strides reduced the prerogatives of the crown and the privileges of the nobility to the limits it judged compatible with the principles of a free government, while raising itself to the rank and consequence of a coequal branch of the legislature. In one instance it has been able to abolish both the royalty and the aristocracy and to overturn all the ancient establishments, in Church as well as State. On a recent occasion it has been able to make the monarch tremble at the prospect of an innovation(1) it attempted. If all this is so, what would be to be feared from an elective chief executive with a four-year term and the confined authorities of a President of the United States? Only that he might be unequal to the task the Constitution assigns him. I shall add only this: if his term is such as to leave a doubt about his firmness, that doubt is inconsistent with a jealousy of his encroachments.
